research_questions: How can a prompt encode which body part contacts which object part without assuming that object presence proves contact?
How should grip, hand occupancy, task, object scale, declared mass, and non-hand support constrain one another?
Which contact facts are visible in a still image, and which must remain resource or compatibility metadata?
How can the same contact grammar extend to nonhuman embodiments without treating human hand datasets as universal anatomy?

mechanisms.statement: AffordPose associates part-level affordance labels such as twist, pull, and handle-grasp with detailed hand poses and computed hand-object contacts.
BEHAVE represents human-object interaction through annotated 3D surface contacts between full-body human and object meshes across varied common-object actions.
Represent each selected contact as an observable body-part to object-part pair, keeping the task label and contact geometry distinct.
Select a grip only after the event task and functional object part are known, so the grasp does not block the part needed for the depicted action.
Treat each hand or equivalent manipulator as a claimed resource and reject simultaneous incompatible claims even when each prop is individually plausible.
Use depicted scale, declared mass, and available support points as compatibility gates; do not infer exact weight or strength from category labels or dataset frequency.
Allow forearm, elbow, shoulder, torso, lap, foot, tail, wing, or environmental support only when the embodiment exposes that capability and the contact remains physically legible.
Expose at least one unobscured contact boundary for contact-critical events and keep resource-only constraints out of the visible prompt candidate list.

candidate_definitions.usc_contact_observable_hand_part_contact: A named hand, finger, palm, or equivalent manipulator visibly meets a named functional region of one prop.
candidate_definitions.usc_contact_task_aligned_grip: A visually specified grasp family and contact region compatible with the selected action, without claiming a medically or mechanically exact grip.
candidate_definitions.usc_contact_two_hand_support_pattern: Two manipulators occupy distinct visible support or control regions on the same object, with no unexplained duplicate occupancy.
candidate_definitions.usc_contact_nonhand_support_point: A visible secondary contact between the prop and an available body segment or environmental support surface.
candidate_definitions.usc_contact_hand_occupancy_claim: A nonvisual metric recording how many manipulators the selected event phase occupies, by owner and claimant, without reserving or authorizing a resource by itself.
candidate_definitions.usc_contact_object_load_claim: A nonvisual metric recording approximate object scale, mass, support demand, and salience burden without deciding eligibility by itself.
candidate_definitions.usc_contact_reachable_contact_guard: A guard requiring the contact point to fall within the embodiment's declared reach, joint, and support capabilities.
candidate_definitions.usc_contact_contact_readability_gate: A guard requiring at least one contact-critical body-object boundary to survive the requested crop and inspection size.

pixel_evidence_definitions.usc_contact_observable_hand_part_contact: At native inspection size, a continuous hand-or-manipulator contour terminates against one identifiable object part with no visible gap or intervening surface.
pixel_evidence_definitions.usc_contact_task_aligned_grip: The thumb, palm, fingers, claws, or equivalent effectors visibly wrap, pinch, brace, hook, or press the declared part while leaving the operative region consistent with the action.
pixel_evidence_definitions.usc_contact_two_hand_support_pattern: Both manipulators and their separate contact zones are visible, and the object orientation or deformation is consistent with two-point support or control.
pixel_evidence_definitions.usc_contact_nonhand_support_point: A second body segment or environmental surface visibly bears, braces, carries, or stabilizes the object rather than merely overlapping it in projection.

compatibility: A one-hand task-aligned grip is compatible with a second free-hand gesture only when occupancy claims reserve different manipulators.
Two-hand support is compatible with medium or high load only when both contact regions and the object's supported orientation are visible.
A non-hand support point is compatible with large or awkward props when the embodiment and pose expose the supporting segment.
Contact candidates are compatible with near, middle, or far semantic-distance props only after the event supplies a functional body-part to object-part edge.
Contact readability may be satisfied by one decisive contact zone while other resource claims remain nonvisual metadata.
conflicts: One manipulator cannot simultaneously grip two separated props unless an explicit multi-object grasp candidate and feasible geometry are selected.
A grip that covers the blade, trigger, opening, hot surface, or other task-critical region conflicts with an action that requires that region to remain usable or safe.
A large or declared-heavy object with no ground, body, second-hand, suspension, or environmental support conflicts with the load gate.
Projected overlap without a continuous contact boundary conflicts with an asserted physical hold, handoff, push, or pull.
A human-hand grip family conflicts with an embodiment that has no compatible manipulator unless a typed translation is supplied.
counterexamples: A prop resting on a table can participate as a target without any hand contact candidate.
An explicitly telekinetic or remote-control event may close physical contact while requiring a visible non-contact causal carrier.
A cropped face portrait may legitimately close contact and prop slots rather than invent off-frame hands.
A broad stylized mitten or chibi artifact may show only a brace or hook relation, not finger-level anatomy.
An object can be carried in a basket, sling, holster, mouth, tail, or platform without consuming a human hand resource.
boundaries: Do not infer strength, dexterity, handedness, disability, pain, competence, occupation, or intent from a depicted grip.
Do not claim exact forces, mass, stability, injury risk, weapon readiness, or safe operation from pixels alone.
Object presence, hand proximity, or silhouette overlap is not sufficient evidence of physical contact.
Dataset labels describe captured or constructed interactions and must not be treated as exhaustive natural human behavior.
When a user explicitly closes empty-hand, no-prop, or no-contact slots, universal contact candidates must remain absent.
domain_limits: AffordPose studies hand-centered affordances on selected 3D objects and BEHAVE covers twenty common objects in captured natural-environment interactions; neither is a complete ontology for fantasy, industrial, medical, weapon, ritual, or assistive domains.
The sources provide contact geometry and pose evidence but do not provide a general physical simulator, exact object mass labels, force closure for humans, or illustration salience thresholds.
Translation from 3D interaction datasets to a single-frame illustration prompt is a design layer that requires holdout validation.
embodiment_limits: Human hand and SMPL-body annotations cannot be copied directly onto faceless, limbless, quadrupedal, winged, tailed, tentacled, robotic, or multi-limbed subjects.
Runtime must query declared manipulators, reach, joints, load-bearing surfaces, support needs, and occupied resources before selecting contact atoms.
Assistive devices, prostheses, mobility aids, and alternative grips must be used only when requested or provided, without treating them as deficits or personality cues.
For nonhuman bodies, translate the functional relation such as wrap, brace, hook, pinch, carry, or support rather than forcing five-finger anatomy.
cultural_limits: Grip, hand choice, touch, carrying practice, tool use, and acceptable body contact can vary by culture and task; the two sources do not establish universal social norms.
Do not attach moral, ritual, gendered, class, or occupational meaning to a contact pattern without explicit context and separate evidence.
Left-right preference and gesture conventions must remain user- or context-specified rather than inferred from dataset prevalence.
source_biases: AffordPose uses manually adjusted hand poses and selected objects with annotated affordances, so it may encode curator choices rather than the full diversity of spontaneous grips.

BEHAVE contains about fifteen thousand annotated frames, eight subjects, five locations, and twenty common objects; its full-body surface contacts do not cover all bodies, environments, object scales, or action purposes.
Both sources prioritize computer-vision or interaction modeling objectives, not illustration aesthetics, accessibility practice, occupational ergonomics, or safety certification.
runtime_implications: Resolve event task and functional object part before selecting grip; then emit one typed body-part to object-part contact edge.
Maintain per-manipulator occupancy, per-object support demand, approximate scale and declared mass, and contact salience as resource claims evaluated before seed-based ranking.
Keep resource claims and compatibility guards out of visual prompt atoms; surface only the smallest contact description needed to make the event legible.
If no feasible contact survives embodiment and slot gates, fail closed or choose a non-contact event rather than inventing anatomy or support.
evaluation_implications: Mutation tests should reject double-booked hands, task-blocking grips, unsupported high-load objects, unreachable contact points, and human-only grips on incompatible bodies.
Metadata-free native review must identify actor or body part, object part, contact relation, and support pattern; projected overlap alone fails.
Thumbnail review is required only when contact is a promise-bearing cue at that output size; otherwise the pack must not claim thumbnail contact legibility.
Holdouts should include empty-hand, no-prop, one-hand, two-hand, non-hand support, nonhuman manipulator, large-prop, and remote non-contact cases.

title: AffordPose: A Large-Scale Dataset of Hand-Object Interactions with Affordance-Driven Hand Pose
authority: IEEE/CVF ICCV 2023 open-access proceedings; authors introduce and analyze the AffordPose dataset
limitations: The dataset uses manually adjusted hand poses rather than unconstrained natural capture for every interaction.
Its part-level affordances and object sample are not an exhaustive catalog of tasks, cultures, hand anatomies, tools, or safety conditions.
It does not establish full-body load paths, exact mass, per-hand runtime occupancy, or still-image salience requirements.
Contact and pose statistics support interaction modeling, not claims about user intent, skill, strength, or social meaning.

title: BEHAVE: Dataset and Method for Tracking Human Object Interactions
authority: IEEE/CVF CVPR 2022 open-access proceedings; authors introduce multi-view full-body human-object data and annotated contacts
limitations: BEHAVE reports about fifteen thousand frames from eight subjects, five locations, and twenty common objects, so coverage is bounded.
Annotated surface contact does not by itself establish force, exact load, task success, safety, or emotional meaning.
SMPL-centered human body modeling does not represent all bodies, assistive devices, clothing contact, or nonhuman anatomies.
The dataset is designed for 3D tracking and reconstruction, not prompt salience, thumbnail readability, or visual storytelling.

research_questions: Which multi-actor relations can be encoded only from visible distance, position, orientation, target, contact, and action direction?
How can shared attention or access be staged without treating gaze or proximity as proof of a private relationship?
What minimum actor-object-actor evidence makes an exchange or reciprocal action legible in one frame?
How should relation edges be bounded in ensembles so every selected relation remains visually attributable?

mechanisms.statement: F-formation detection operationalizes free-standing group structure from people's positions and orientations around an accessible shared space.
The F-formation model describes an o-space to which participants have direct and comparatively equal access, while recognizing multiple spatial arrangements.
H2O records human-human object handovers with giver hand-object states, receiver grasps, object pose, and the evolving transfer interaction.
H2O treats pre-handover giver state and receiver grasp as distinct observable parts of a transfer rather than a single undifferentiated social label.
Represent shared focus as multiple visible orientation or action edges converging on the same object or bounded area, not as an inferred shared belief.
Represent reciprocity only when two or more directed actions answer one another in the depicted phase, such as extend and receive, brace and pull, or point and reorient.
Keep romance, kinship, friendship, dominance, personality, consent, trust, hostility, and group membership outside automatic relation inference unless explicitly supplied by the user.
Select the smallest connected actor-target graph that explains the scene and reject ensemble edges whose endpoints or direction cannot be read.

candidate_definitions.usc_relation_distance_orientation_edge: A visual edge recording relative actor position and body, head, or available directional orientation without assigning social meaning.
candidate_definitions.usc_relation_shared_access_region: A bounded open or occupied scene region that two or more actors visibly face, reach toward, or arrange around.
candidate_definitions.usc_relation_shared_target_convergence: Two or more gaze, head, torso, pointing, reaching, or tool-action vectors terminate at one visible target.
candidate_definitions.usc_relation_giver_object_receiver_chain: A visible giver-to-object and object-to-receiver chain with distinct hands or manipulators and a readable transfer phase.
candidate_definitions.usc_relation_reciprocal_action_pair: Two directed visible actions whose endpoints answer one another within the same event, without inferring the actors' private relationship.
candidate_definitions.usc_relation_relation_truth_guard: A nonvisual inference guard prohibiting automatic claims about romance, dominance, personality, kinship, friendship, consent, trust, hostility, or persistent group identity.
candidate_definitions.usc_relation_actor_target_edge_budget: A composition guard limiting relation edges to a sparse connected graph whose actors, targets, and directions remain attributable.

pixel_evidence_definitions.usc_relation_distance_orientation_edge: At least two actors have separable silhouettes and readable relative positions plus one directional carrier such as torso, head, feet, or limb orientation; no social label is required.
pixel_evidence_definitions.usc_relation_shared_access_region: A common object or bounded negative-space region lies within the visible facing or reaching field of every claimed participant.
pixel_evidence_definitions.usc_relation_shared_target_convergence: At least two independently traceable directional vectors terminate on the same visible object or area, and each vector has an identifiable actor origin.
pixel_evidence_definitions.usc_relation_giver_object_receiver_chain: The object sits between distinct giver and receiver manipulators; one supports or offers while the other approaches, contacts, or has just received it, with no ambiguous third hand.
pixel_evidence_definitions.usc_relation_reciprocal_action_pair: Two actor-originated action paths visibly meet, counter, continue, or answer each other at a shared target or exchange boundary.

compatibility: Distance and orientation edges are compatible with a shared access region when actor silhouettes and the common region remain unobstructed.
Shared target convergence is compatible with gaze-free embodiments when torso, limb, tool, beam, or locomotion direction supplies independent visible vectors.
A giver-object-receiver chain is compatible with reciprocal action when giver support and receiver approach or grasp occupy distinct readable phases or roles.
Dyads may use one reciprocal edge pair; ensembles may use a shared target or short exchange chain when the edge budget preserves attribution.
Observable relation atoms may accompany any topic route because they describe staging edges rather than persistent character identity.
conflicts: Proximity or face-to-face orientation conflicts with any automatic claim of romance, intimacy, friendship, dominance, aggression, consent, or personality.
A shared target claim conflicts with actors whose visible directional carriers terminate on different objects or off-frame regions.
An exchange claim conflicts with an object merely located between actors when neither actor has a readable give, receive, contact, or support edge.
Reciprocity conflicts with a one-sided action whose second actor is passive, occluded, or visually unrelated in the selected phase.
A dense all-to-all ensemble relation graph conflicts with endpoint attribution and sparse event composition.
counterexamples: Two strangers facing the same display may share an observable target without sharing friendship, affiliation, or intent.
Two close actors may be constrained by a crowded environment; distance alone does not prove intimacy.
A romantic pair may stand side by side with no pixel-visible romantic cue, so the relation can be user-fixed while universal visual relation slots remain minimal.
An actor looking off-frame may attend to an unseen target, but a still image cannot claim shared attention unless another visible carrier supports the same target.
A row of performers facing the camera has common orientation but not necessarily an interaction or reciprocal relation.
boundaries: Never infer romance, sexual orientation, kinship, friendship, dominance, submissiveness, personality, trust, consent, hostility, guilt, deception, or durable group membership from spacing, gaze, pose, clothing, or contact.
Use relation labels only as staging descriptions of visible edges in the depicted moment unless the user explicitly fixes a narrative relationship.
Do not treat lack of eye contact, physical distance, mobility configuration, assistive technology, or atypical body orientation as social withdrawal or diminished agency.
Do not convert dataset action labels into moral or psychological truth.
When a relation, interaction, gaze, or multi-actor slot is explicitly closed, do not introduce a universal relation candidate.
domain_limits: The F-formation source focuses on free-standing conversational groups and proxemic group detection; it does not cover every crowd, combat, performance, caregiving, ritual, vehicle, or remote interaction.
H2O focuses on human-human object handover videos with fifteen people and thirty objects; it is not a general theory of cooperation, reciprocity, or social relationships.
Neither source defines illustration crop, salience, or narrative truth, and temporal evidence must be reduced cautiously to one selected still phase.
embodiment_limits: Eye gaze may be unavailable or ambiguous for faceless, masked, helmeted, eyeless, nonhuman, or very small subjects; use head, torso, limb, tool, light, locomotion, or contact direction when available.
Relative distance and orientation must be measured against each embodiment's scale, mobility, support, sensory channels, and accessible reach rather than a single human standing template.
Wheelchairs, mobility aids, prostheses, seated bodies, quadrupeds, multi-limbed bodies, and asymmetric bodies require capability-aware relation carriers without negative social inference.
A giver-receiver chain requires distinguishable manipulators and object ownership states, not necessarily human hands.
cultural_limits: Interpersonal distance, facing angle, eye contact, touch, offering etiquette, and handover conventions vary across cultures, settings, roles, and accessibility needs.
The F-formation datasets and H2O captures cannot establish universal personal-space thresholds or preferred exchange hands.
Culture-specific gestures or status conventions require separate evidence and explicit context; they must not be inferred from actor appearance or names.
source_biases: F-formation detection reduces a socially rich encounter to position and orientation and evaluates a limited set of recorded group settings; that reduction is useful for observable staging but insufficient for relationship truth.
H2O is a purpose-built handover benchmark with bounded participants, objects, capture conditions, and task roles; it privileges successful transfer sequences over broader social interaction.
Both sources center human visual behavior and computer-vision labels, underrepresenting nonvisual communication, disability variation, nonhuman embodiments, and culture-specific practices.
runtime_implications: Build a typed actor-target graph from visible or user-fixed edges: relative pose, shared region, shared target, contact, give, receive, support, or counteraction.
Apply the relation truth guard before lexical realization so topology never silently becomes romance, dominance, personality, or other private-state language.
For shared targets, require at least two independent origin-to-target carriers; for exchange, require giver-object and object-receiver edges plus a selected phase.
Bound relation edges by actor count and salience, choosing one readable spine rather than independently sampling pair labels.
evaluation_implications: Mutation tests should reject proximity-to-romance, height-to-dominance, gaze-aversion-to-hostility, object-between-actors-to-handover, and one-sided-action-to-reciprocity rewrites.
Metadata-free review must identify each claimed actor, target, edge direction, and exchange or reciprocal boundary without reading narrative labels.
Holdouts should cover strangers sharing a target, explicit partners with neutral staging, faceless actors, nonhuman actors, seated or aided bodies, dyad handover, and ensemble shared focus.
A relation pack passes only on observable topology; reviewers must not score whether the inferred social story feels true.

title: F-Formation Detection: Individuating Free-Standing Conversational Groups in Images
authority: PLOS ONE research article with methods, datasets, code availability, correction linkage, and experiments on position-orientation group detection
limitations: The operational target is free-standing conversational group detection, not every type of social, task, or narrative relation.
Position and orientation can support a staging hypothesis but cannot establish romance, dominance, personality, intent, consent, or durable affiliation.
The study evaluates several bounded datasets and reports sensitivity to position and orientation noise.
Its common o-space concept does not require or prove eye gaze, mutual belief, emotional agreement, or object exchange.

title: H2O: A Benchmark for Visual Human-Human Object Handover Analysis
authority: IEEE/CVF ICCV 2021 open-access proceedings; authors introduce an eighteen-thousand-clip human-human object-handover benchmark
limitations: H2O contains a bounded sample of fifteen people and thirty objects performing handover tasks, not all cultures, bodies, objects, or collaboration modes.
A handover benchmark does not support claims about the actors' relationship, motives, trust, consent, personality, or status.
Video evidence contains temporal phases that may not all be legible in one frozen illustration frame.
Receiver-grasp prediction and pose metrics do not define visual salience, composition, or universal ergonomic safety.

research_questions: How should user prop terms be sense-disambiguated into canonical concepts without treating strings as visual evidence?
How can synonyms, broader and narrower classes, and whole-part relations improve retrieval while preserving the user's specificity?
How should era, culture, language, and source disagreement remain typed metadata rather than inferred visual truth?
Which lexical relations may route to a prop catalog, and which must never be emitted as prompt candidates?

mechanisms.statement: Open English WordNet groups lexical entries into sense-specific synsets and links them through relations including synonymy, hypernymy, antonymy, and meronymy.
Getty AAT represents unique concepts with terms, scope notes, parent contexts, sources, and equivalence, hierarchical, and associative relations, including multilingual terms.
Normalize an input form to a sense-qualified concept only after aliases and scope evidence distinguish homonyms, polysemy, and unbound compounds.
Use broader classes for retrieval fallback and compatibility inheritance, but never replace a user-specified narrower prop with a generic class in the realized scene.
Store component, member, substance, and generic whole-part links as typed relations so a part is not silently treated as the complete object.
Getty AAT provides concepts and metadata for styles, periods, cultures, materials, activities, and objects, but its scopes are cataloging contexts rather than automatic visual prescriptions.
Retain unresolved senses, missing aliases, conflicting broader contexts, and source gaps as uncertainty that blocks or down-ranks routing rather than guessing.
Keep canonical IDs, alias sets, hypernym chains, part links, era metadata, and culture-language metadata nonvisual; only a separately selected concrete prop atom may enter the prompt or pixel rubric.

candidate_definitions.usc_lexical_canonical_concept_id: A nonvisual stable identifier for one disambiguated generic prop concept, separate from any display string or generated image atom.
candidate_definitions.usc_lexical_synonym_alias_set: A nonvisual set of same-concept labels with source, language, preferred or variant status, and confidence.
candidate_definitions.usc_lexical_hypernym_chain: A nonvisual ordered set of broader classes used for retrieval and typed compatibility fallback without erasing the requested narrower concept.
candidate_definitions.usc_lexical_part_whole_links: Nonvisual typed component, member, substance, or generic whole-part edges between canonical concepts.
candidate_definitions.usc_lexical_era_scope_metadata: Nonvisual asserted, historical, approximate, disputed, or unknown period applicability with source provenance.
candidate_definitions.usc_lexical_culture_language_scope_metad: Nonvisual culture, region, language, translation, and usage scope with explicit uncertainty and source provenance.
candidate_definitions.usc_lexical_sense_ambiguity_guard: A guard that blocks automatic routing when an input has multiple materially different senses and context does not resolve them.
candidate_definitions.usc_lexical_source_disagreement_guard: A guard that records conflicting equivalence, hierarchy, part, era, or culture claims instead of flattening them into one asserted fact.

compatibility: A canonical concept is compatible with an alias only when both sources or an authoritative scope note support the same sense, or the mapping retains explicit uncertainty.
A hypernym chain is compatible with retrieval fallback while the final selected prop preserves every user-fixed narrower constraint.
A part link is compatible with visual realization only when another candidate specifies whether the part, whole, or exposed assembly is actually depicted.
Era and culture metadata are compatible with soft-prior ranking or typed gates when explicitly requested, sourced, and not inferred from character appearance.
Lexical routers are compatible with every topic route because they normalize input before visual candidate selection and contribute no visual salience themselves.
conflicts: Collapsing homonyms or materially different senses into one canonical concept conflicts with sense-qualified routing.
Replacing a requested machine gun with the broader class weapon, or a requested apple with the broader class food, conflicts with specificity preservation.
Treating a handle, trigger, blade, lid, or wheel as the complete object conflicts with typed part-whole semantics unless the part itself is requested.
Using a historical, cultural, translated, disputed, or preferred catalog term as direct pixel evidence conflicts with the nonvisual router-only rule.
Automatically emitting every alias, parent, part, era, or culture label into the prompt conflicts with sparse visual composition.
counterexamples: Apple may denote a fruit or a proper-name organization; an unresolved string cannot route to the fruit prop solely because the image domain often contains food.
Hammer may denote a tool family while claw hammer is a narrower subtype; the broader term is useful for fallback but cannot add a claw not requested or selected.
Gun and machine gun are not interchangeable levels of specificity, and taxonomy membership does not establish scene safety, readiness, era, or narrative role.
A preferred English catalog label is not automatically the preferred term in another language or community.
A lexical part relation such as chair has part backrest does not prove that the backrest is visible, intact, separately manipulable, or relevant in the generated frame.
boundaries: Lexical metadata is not a visual atom, prompt decoration, pixel claim, affordance, safety judgment, narrative role, or cultural truth.
Do not infer era, culture, nationality, class, religion, gender, occupation, or identity from a prop term or a character's appearance.
Do not treat source inclusion as legal clearance, historical certainty, trademark permission, authenticity certification, or universal contemporary usage.
Preserve user wording when disambiguation is unresolved; ask, fail closed, or expose alternatives rather than silently choosing a materially different sense.
Proper names, protected franchise objects, named brands, and living-culture terminology require separate governance beyond this generic prop lexicon.
domain_limits: Open English WordNet is an English general lexical network and does not supply complete multilingual, specialist, historical, visual, or culture-specific prop coverage.
Getty AAT is scoped to art, architecture, material culture, conservation, and related cataloging; it explicitly excludes many out-of-domain or unwarranted terms and is not comprehensive.
Neither source defines prop affordances, physical compatibility, image salience, safety policy, narrative fit, or prompt effectiveness.
A combined lexical router still requires a separate curated universal prop catalog with typed visual, event, resource, and guard data.
embodiment_limits: Canonical object identity does not imply that a subject can reach, grip, carry, wear, operate, perceive, or safely use the object.
Part names must resolve against object geometry and embodiment capabilities before contact or action candidates are selected.
Lexical relations must not encode human-hand assumptions or exclude alternative manipulators, assistive devices, mounts, containers, supports, or remote operation.
An object's language or cultural label cannot be used to infer the embodiment, identity, or ability of the depicted subject.
cultural_limits: Synonymy and translation are not identical: terms may differ in register, period, region, community preference, taboo, or conceptual boundary.
AAT multilingual and culture metadata improve scope but do not guarantee equal coverage, local authority, present-day preference, or community consent.
Culture and era fields must be explicit, sourced, revisable metadata with unknown and disputed states, never visual stereotypes.
Cross-language alias expansion should preserve the original user term and confidence rather than imposing an English canonical display label.
source_biases: Open English WordNet is derived from Princeton WordNet and developed as an English lexical resource; relation density and sense distinctions vary across domains, and English structure is not a universal ontology.
Getty AAT grows through institutional and expert contributions in cultural-heritage cataloging, so coverage follows collection, contributor, language, and disciplinary priorities.
The two resources model lexical and cataloging relations, not how ordinary viewers name every depicted object or how image models realize those words.
Agreement between the sources increases routing confidence but does not prove visual equivalence, cultural neutrality, or exhaustive correctness.
runtime_implications: Resolve input strings to sense-qualified canonical IDs before sampling props; retain the original term, matched aliases, sources, and confidence in the trace.
Use hypernyms for candidate retrieval and compatibility inheritance, part links for object-part targeting, and era or culture metadata only for requested soft priors or typed gates.
Do not put any usc_lexical candidate ID, alias list, hierarchy label, or scope metadata into visual atoms, composed prompt prose, or pixel evidence.

When ambiguity or source disagreement changes the likely prop, fail closed, ask for clarification when permitted, or expose deterministic alternatives; do not use creativity to override the ambiguity guard.
evaluation_implications: Schema tests must require an empty pixel evidence subset for this topic and reject any lexical-router candidate assigned a visual role.

Mutation tests should cover homonyms, narrower-to-broader substitution, whole-part inversion, unsupported translation, disputed era, culture inference, and alias keyword leakage into composed prompts.
Round-trip tests should show that multiple valid aliases route to one canonical ID while preserving the user's original wording and that one ambiguous form can remain unresolved.
Visual qualification should evaluate only the concrete prop atom chosen downstream; the lexical router itself has no metadata-free pixel success claim.

title: Open English WordNet
authority: Open English WordNet community resource linked by the Global WordNet Association and maintained as the open-source successor derived from Princeton WordNet
limitations: The resource is English-centered and cannot establish multilingual equivalence, local usage, culture, or era by itself.
Relation coverage and sense granularity vary across lexical domains and may differ from ordinary or specialist visual naming.
A synset or lexical relation does not prove object visibility, affordance, physical compatibility, narrative fit, safety, or prompt effectiveness.
The resource's open-source evolution means version identity and provenance must be recorded for deterministic production use.

title: General Information About the Art and Architecture Thesaurus
authority: Getty Research Institute official AAT editorial guidelines describing concept IDs, terms, sources, notes, multilinguality, and equivalence, hierarchical, and associative relations
limitations: AAT is scoped to art, architecture, material culture, conservation, and related cataloging and explicitly excludes many out-of-domain terms.
It is evolving and contribution-driven rather than comprehensive or equally representative across languages, cultures, periods, and object domains.
Preferred terms and hierarchical positions are cataloging decisions with scope and warrant, not automatic visual prescriptions or community-wide usage mandates.
The guidelines do not define image salience, object affordance, embodiment compatibility, safety, narrative role, or generative-prompt quality.
